source.title: Timbuctoo the Mysterious
source.attribution: Félix Dubois, Timbuctoo the Mysterious (trans. Diana White), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Djenné's island site kept it unconquered for centuries
cards.body:
Djenné, in what is now central Mali, was founded around 765 according to the chronicles Dubois used, on an island ringed by channels of the Niger and Bani rivers. High banks, a wall and the yearly floods made it very hard to attack.

Dubois found that people there told him their city had never been taken by storm. The Tarikh es-Sudan, written in Timbuktu in the 1650s, agrees, saying the Mali empire fought Djenné nearly a hundred times without winning. Even the most powerful neighbour could not crack a well-chosen position.

The lesson carries over: where you place yourself, whether a business, a home or a career, can protect you more than constant fighting.
cards.quote: There were many battles, nearly a hundred, and the people of Jenne were always victorious.
cards.apply_it: Think of one choice of position you could make (where you work, live or sell) that would make problems less likely in the first place.

quiz.question: According to the Tarikh es-Sudan, how did Djenné fare against the Mali empire?
options: It was conquered in the first battle
It won nearly a hundred battles and was never taken
It paid tribute to avoid any fighting
It moved the whole city to a new island
quiz.explanation: The chronicle says the people of Djenné won nearly a hundred battles and the Malinke never came back for the hundredth.

cards.title: A city's founding prayer: let the poor stranger prosper here
cards.body:
Around 1050, the chief of Djenné, Koumbourou, became a Muslim. The Tarikh says he called together more than four thousand scholars and asked them to pray for three things for his town.

The first was striking: that anyone who arrived there poor, having left a homeland where he could not make a living, should find life so easy that he forgot where he came from. Only then did he ask for trade and wealth. He then pulled down his own palace and built a great mosque on the spot.

Djenné did grow into one of the richest market towns of West Africa. A place that sets out to welcome newcomers and give them a chance tends to draw energy and talent to it.
cards.quote: That any person who should arrive there, having quitted his country from poverty and an inability to live in it, should receive from God such abundant and easy means of life that he should forget his native land.
cards.apply_it: Is there a newcomer at your work, school or street you could help get a foothold this week?

quiz.question: What did Koumbourou ask the scholars to pray for first?
options: That no strangers would ever settle there
That poor newcomers would prosper in the town
quiz.explanation: His first wish was that anyone who came to Djenné in poverty would find an easy living there; trade and wealth came after.

cards.title: Timbuktu began as a herders' camp beside a good well
cards.body:
The Tarikh tells that around 1100 a Tuareg group grazed their herds between the Sahara and the Niger. They found a sheltered pool with good water and set up a fixed camp, with a thorn fence against wild animals. The stores were left in the care of an old woman, and the place took its name, Tomboutou, from her nickname.

Travellers began to stop there. Caravans heading for the Mali kingdom refilled their supplies, a market sprang up, and people built permanent houses.

Great cities often start small: a reliable source of water, a safe stop on a route, someone trustworthy keeping watch. Small, dependable services draw people, and people draw everything else.
cards.quote: Caravans coming from the north and east (Algeria and Tripoli) on their way to the Mali kingdom delayed at the camp to renew their stores.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Timbuctoo Across the Centuries ¶19
cards.apply_it: What small, reliable thing could you offer that would make people keep coming back to you?

quiz.question: According to the tradition Dubois recorded, why did Timbuktu first attract travellers?
options: It was a safe camp with water where caravans could restock
quiz.explanation: The camp offered water and supplies, so passing caravans stopped, and a market grew around them.

cards.title: Djenné and Timbuktu worked as two halves of one trading city
cards.body:
Timbuktu sat at the edge of the desert, where salt caravans from the Sahara arrived. Djenné, about twenty days upstream, sat among farmland that produced grain, gold and cloth. Dubois explains that Djenné's merchants settled in Timbuktu to buy salt at first hand and ship it south in their big river boats.

People in the region had a saying for it: the two towns were halves of one city. Djenné was the producer and wholesaler; Timbuktu was the warehouse and meeting point with traders from North Africa.

Many successful ventures pair two different strengths, one close to the source and one close to the buyer, and both do better than either would alone.
cards.quote: The Sudanese express this idea in their saying: ‘Jenne and Timbuctoo are two halves of the same city.
cards.apply_it: Who could be your 'other half': someone whose strengths cover a gap in yours? Reach out to them this week.

quiz.question: What role did Djenné play compared with Timbuktu?
options: Djenné was the producing and shipping centre; Timbuktu was the depot facing the desert
The two cities were rivals that never traded
quiz.explanation: Djenné's merchants shipped goods north and kept agents in Timbuktu, where desert caravans brought salt.

cards.title: Djenné's merchants let people with nothing sell on commission
cards.body:
Dubois describes Djenné's trading houses as real firms. They had agents in other towns, branches in Timbuktu and travelling salesmen paid a percentage of what they sold.

An old merchant explained the system to him. They handed goods to people who had none, those people sold them around the country and kept part of the profit. Anyone willing to work could save up and become a merchant in turn. He added that begging was a disgrace there, because everyone could earn a living.

Commission selling, franchising and apprenticeships work on the same idea: lend people the stock or the tools before they can afford them, and you widen the circle of those who can build something.
cards.quote: We trust our merchandise to people who have no goods; they sell it for us throughout the country, and part of the profit is theirs. If they have the will they can become merchants in their turn.
cards.apply_it: Is there a way you could give someone a start (a lead, a tool, a first job) that lets them grow into a peer?

quiz.question: How could a poor person in Djenné become a merchant, according to the old trader?
options: By selling a merchant's goods on commission and saving the profit
quiz.explanation: Merchants trusted goods to people without any, who sold them and kept part of the profit until they could trade on their own.

cards.title: Mansa Musa of Mali added Timbuktu to his empire after his pilgrimage
cards.body:
In the early 1300s the Mali empire, based in the western part of present-day Mali, was at its height under Mansa Musa, whom Dubois calls Kounkour-Moussa. Timbuktu's Tuareg overlords had been taxing the town ever harder, so the people invited the Mali king to take it over.

Musa came on his way back from his famous pilgrimage to Mecca. Dubois dates his arrival to 1330; modern historians usually say about 1325. He gave the main mosque a pyramid-shaped minaret, built himself a palace, and left a governor.

Rule that squeezes people too hard makes them look for someone else. Mali gained a great city partly because the old rulers had made themselves unwelcome.
cards.quote: He, being just returned from the conquest of the Songhois and a pilgrimage to Mecca, entered Timbuctoo in 1330. He presented the Cathedral Mosque with a minaret of pyramidal form, built himself a palace, and installed a governor there upon his departure.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Timbuctoo Across the Centuries ¶22
cards.apply_it: Where are you asking too much of someone (a customer, colleague or family member)? Ease off before they look elsewhere.

quiz.question: Why did the people of Timbuktu invite the king of Mali to take over the town?
options: Their Tuareg rulers kept raising taxes
They wanted to go on pilgrimage
Mali threatened to burn the town
quiz.explanation: Rising demands from the Tuareg governors pushed the townspeople to invite Mansa Musa in.

cards.title: Ali Kolon planned his escape from the Mali court for years
cards.body:
When Songhai, centred on Gao in present-day Mali, became a vassal of Mali, two young Songhai princes, Ali Kolon and his brother, were kept at the Mali court, as vassals' sons often were.

The Tarikh calls Ali Kolon prudent and thoughtful. He offered to travel on royal business, going a little further each time and learning the roads home. He hid weapons and food along the route, and the brothers trained their horses for endurance. When they finally fled, pursuers caught them, but they fought them off and reached home. Ali Kolon was made king with the title Sunni, 'the Liberator'.

Big escapes, from a job, a debt or a bad situation, usually rest on quiet preparation long before the day you leave.
cards.quote: He was an intelligent youth, full of prudence, reflection, and enlightenment. By prolonging each journey a little further he learned to know the roads of the country, and, above all, those leading towards Songhoi.
cards.apply_it: Write down one exit you might need one day, and take one small step this week to prepare for it.

quiz.question: How did Ali Kolon prepare his escape?
options: He waited for the king to die
He asked his father to send an army
He learned the roads on official journeys and hid supplies along the way
quiz.explanation: He used his travels to learn the routes and stash arms and food, then trained the horses before fleeing.

cards.title: 'If you cannot defend Timbuktu, stop occupying it'
cards.body:
Mali held Timbuktu for about a century, until the 1430s. As the empire weakened, Tuareg groups began raiding the edges of the town, and the Mali garrison did not dare to fight back.

The Tuareg chief Akil then sent the Mali officials a blunt message: if you cannot defend Timbuktu, stop occupying it. They left.

The story makes a point about any position of authority. People accept a ruler, a manager or a leader largely because that person protects them and keeps things working. When the protection stops, the title soon goes too. Authority is something you keep earning, not something you simply hold.
cards.quote: If you cannot defend Timbuctoo, cease to occupy it.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Timbuctoo Across the Centuries ¶23
cards.apply_it: List the people who rely on you. For each one, ask: am I still doing the job that gives me standing with them?

quiz.question: What happened when Mali could no longer defend Timbuktu?
options: It hired the Tuareg as guards
Its officials withdrew after Akil's message
quiz.explanation: Faced with raids they would not resist, the Mali officials left when the Tuareg chief told them to.

cards.title: Timbuktu's patron saint kept trading so he would owe no one
cards.body:
Sidi Yahya (1373 to 1462) was a scholar, judge and teacher in Timbuktu, later honoured as the city's patron saint. The chronicles say he gave away the gifts people brought him, cleaned up corruption in the courts and taught for fifty years.

One story shows a practical streak. Asked why his visions of the Prophet had grown rare, he guessed it was because he now spent time on trade. Then why do it? 'Because I have no wish to be dependent on others,' he answered.

Even a deeply spiritual life, in this story, has room for earning your own keep. Paying your own way can be a form of freedom that lets you speak and act honestly.
cards.quote: But why do you do so?’ ‘Because I have no wish to be dependent on others,
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The University of Sankoré ¶20
cards.apply_it: Is there one area of life where depending on someone limits what you feel free to say or do? Name one step toward standing on your own feet.

quiz.question: Why did Sidi Yahya say he spent time on trade?
options: To become the richest man in Timbuktu
So he would not have to depend on others
To pay for a new mosque
quiz.explanation: He accepted the cost to his devotions because he did not want to rely on anyone else for his living.

cards.title: Sunni Ali built the Songhai empire through twenty years of war
cards.body:
Sunni Ali ruled Songhai from 1464 until his death in the early 1490s. He took Timbuktu (Dubois dates it 1469), besieged Djenné, fought the Mossi to the south and spent most of his reign tearing down what was left of the Mali empire to the west.

The chronicle admits he lost only two campaigns. Dubois judges that he conquered without organising: he took plunder, prisoners and tribute but set up little to hold the land together. The cost in lives was great, and the Muslim chroniclers remembered him as a cruel tyrant. He drowned crossing a stream on his way home from a campaign.

Winning ground and building something lasting are different skills. The next ruler would have to supply the second.
cards.quote: Nevertheless, while fighting from east to west during twenty years, he is unconsciously laying the foundations of Songhoi greatness;
cards.apply_it: Look at a recent 'win' of yours. What would it take to turn it into something that lasts?

quiz.question: What weakness does Dubois see in Sunni Ali's conquests?
options: He lost most of his battles
He conquered widely but did little to organise what he took
quiz.explanation: Dubois says Sunni Ali was busy with plunder and tribute and had no time to give his conquests a durable form.

cards.title: After a years-long siege, Sunni Ali honoured Djenné instead of sacking it
cards.body:
Djenné resisted Sunni Ali longer than anywhere else. Tradition gives the siege as seven years, seven months and seven days; others say four years. His soldiers stayed so long that they took up farming around the town.

When famine finally pushed Djenné's chief to offer peace, Sunni Ali, worn out too, gave generous terms. He seated the former enemy at his right hand, married the chief's mother and left the city unharmed.

A defeated opponent who is treated with respect can become an ally, and the thing you were fighting for stays intact. Djenné remained a prosperous Songhai city for generations.
cards.quote: So far from humiliating it in the day of its capitulation, he seated his former enemy on his right hand, married his mother, and, most important of all as far as we are concerned, he respected the town.
cards.apply_it: Next time you win an argument or a negotiation, give the other side one way to keep their dignity.

quiz.question: How did Sunni Ali treat Djenné when it finally surrendered?
options: He gave honourable terms and spared the town
He burned it to the ground
He sold its people into slavery
He moved its population to Gao
quiz.explanation: He seated Djenné's chief at his right hand and respected the city, which went on to thrive.

cards.title: Ask who wrote the history before you trust its verdict
cards.body:
The scholars who wrote the Sudan's chronicles heaped abuse on Sunni Ali: impious, a tyrant, a destroyer of towns. He did kill many people, including scholars. But Dubois points out what else was going on. The writers were Muslim clerics, and Sunni Ali had been lax about prayer, kept older religious practices and persecuted scholars who plotted against him. The same sources admit he honoured and paid scholars who stayed out of politics.

Dubois's own judgment is coloured by his era, but his method holds up. When a historical figure is painted all black or all white, ask who wrote the record, what they wanted and what they left out.

The same habit helps with news, reviews and office gossip.
cards.quote: The impartiality of history has no concern with these accumulations of abuse; they merely represent the personal venom of his chroniclers.
cards.apply_it: Pick a strong opinion you read this week. Who wrote it, and what might they gain from you believing it?

quiz.question: Why does Dubois think the chroniclers condemned Sunni Ali so harshly?
options: They were clerics angry at his lax religion and his treatment of scholars who opposed him
quiz.explanation: The writers were religious scholars, and their verdict reflected his half-hearted Islam and his clashes with politically active clerics.

cards.title: Sunni Ali's servants learned to delay his angry orders
cards.body:
The Tarikh describes Sunni Ali's temper as violent. In a rage he might order the death of anyone around him, even his most loyal and useful people. His remorse came just as fast.

His servants learned to handle this. When he condemned someone he would later miss, they simply kept that person out of sight until the king calmed down. He was then delighted to find his order had not been carried out. His best general, Mohammed ben Abou Bakr, was condemned this way more than once.

Decisions made in anger are often the ones we most regret. Building in a pause, even if it is only waiting until tomorrow, protects you and the people around you.
cards.quote: His servants were aware of this, and, when the condemned person was one whom Sunni Ali would afterwards regret, they would merely keep him out of sight until the moment of repentance arrived.
cards.apply_it: Make a rule: no angry message gets sent until you have slept on it.

quiz.question: How did Sunni Ali's servants deal with his angry death sentences?
options: They always carried them out at once
They hid the condemned person until his anger passed
They asked the scholars to overrule him
quiz.explanation: Knowing his remorse would follow, they kept people out of sight, and he was glad when his orders had been delayed.

cards.title: Askia Mohammed took the insult 'usurper' as his royal name
cards.body:
After Sunni Ali died, his general Mohammed ben Abou Bakr did not want to go on living under constant threat. He fought Sunni Ali's son, lost the first battle, regrouped and won a long, bloody second one. He took the throne in the 1490s.

According to the Tarikh, when Sunni Ali's daughters heard the news they cried 'Askia!', which Dubois explains as meaning 'it is not he' or 'usurper'. Mohammed's response was to order that he be called by no other name. He became Askia Mohammed, and his whole dynasty carried the title.

Taking ownership of a label meant to wound can rob it of its power. What others call you need not decide what the word comes to mean.
cards.quote: they exclaimed ‘Askia!’ which signifies ‘It is not he,’ or ‘Usurper.’ This being repeated to him, Mohammed ordained that no other surname should be given him, and Askia Mohammed he accordingly became.
cards.apply_it: Is there a label someone has pinned on you? Consider how you could own it rather than fight it.

quiz.question: Where did the title 'Askia' come from, according to the Tarikh?
options: An exclamation meaning 'usurper' by Sunni Ali's daughters
A word for 'great king' in Arabic
The name of Mohammed's home town
A title granted by the caliph
quiz.explanation: Sunni Ali's daughters cried 'Askia!', and Mohammed ordered that this be his only name.

cards.title: Askia Mohammed's pilgrimage left a hostel for West Africans in Mecca
cards.body:
In 1497, once his rule was secure, Askia Mohammed left his brother Omar in charge and set off on pilgrimage to Mecca and Cairo. The Tarikh says he travelled with a thousand foot soldiers and five hundred horsemen, carrying 300,000 mitkals of gold from Sunni Ali's treasury.

He spent much of it in alms at the holy places. In Mecca he bought gardens and founded a charitable house for pilgrims from the Sudan, the lands south of the Sahara. In Cairo the Abbasid caliph named him his representative in the region.

Dubois notes the trip also boosted Askia's legitimacy. Even so, one lasting result was a refuge for ordinary travellers from home, which outlived the gold.
cards.quote: In the latter town he bought gardens and established a charitable institute for the people of the Sudan. This place is well known in Mecca, and cost five thousand mitkals.
cards.apply_it: If you have money or influence to give, ask what would still help ordinary people long after you are gone.

quiz.question: What lasting institution did Askia Mohammed set up in Mecca?
options: A charitable house for pilgrims from the Sudan
quiz.explanation: He bought gardens and founded a charitable institute for the people of the Sudan, well known in Mecca.

cards.title: Askia sought out the great scholars of Cairo and kept asking their advice
cards.body:
While in Cairo, Askia Mohammed spent time with its theologians and scholars, asking how best to live and govern. He paid special attention to al-Suyuti (Dubois writes Essoyouti), one of the most famous writers in Arabic.

The habit did not end when he went home. Askia wrote to al-Suyuti and, Dubois says, always put his most important reforms to him first and followed his advice. Dubois believes the system of government that held Songhai together for a century took shape from these conversations.

A leader does not need to know everything. Finding the best minds you can, and staying in touch with them, is a skill in itself.
cards.quote: Askia opened a correspondence with him on his return to Songhois, and always submitted his most important reforms to the savant, never neglecting to follow his advice concerning them.
cards.apply_it: Name one person who knows more than you about a decision you face. Write to them this week.

quiz.question: What did Askia do after returning from Cairo?
options: Kept writing to al-Suyuti and put major reforms to him
quiz.explanation: He corresponded with al-Suyuti and submitted his most important reforms to him for advice.

cards.title: Askia saw conquered peoples as future partners, at a heavy cost in lives
cards.body:
Between about 1501 and 1513, Dubois says, Askia Mohammed waged a long war on the Mali empire to the west. Mali's capital was destroyed so completely that its site could no longer be found, and the provinces suffered badly. Songhai losses were so heavy that Askia's brother Omar wept and said the Songhai would be wiped out.

Askia replied that the conquered peoples would become part of the Songhai and help them. He did later recruit soldiers and officials from them.

The human cost here was great on both sides, and it should not be glossed over. The idea inside Askia's reply is still worth keeping: people you once opposed can become partners, if you choose to bring them in.
cards.quote: these conquered nations will make our lives easier, for they will become a part of us, and will assist us in our enterprises.
cards.apply_it: Think of a former rival or critic. What would it take to make them a collaborator?

quiz.question: How did Askia answer his brother Omar's fear that the Songhai would be wiped out?
options: He said the conquered peoples would become part of the Songhai and help them
He blamed Omar for the losses
quiz.explanation: He argued the conquered nations would join them and help in their enterprises, and later recruited troops from them.

cards.title: Askia replaced tribute-taking with a real administration
cards.body:
Sunni Ali had been content to demand tribute from the lands he conquered. Askia Mohammed went further. Dubois says he pulled down the old local systems and rebuilt them with his own officials, so his orders were carried out at the far edges of the empire as they were in the palace.

He created four viceroys, each overseeing provincial governors, military chiefs, judges and tax collectors, with top posts held by members or in-laws of the royal family.

Holding territory, a market or a team takes structure: clear roles, people accountable for each area, and decisions that reach the edges. Without that, gains fade as fast as they came.
cards.quote: Unlike Sunni Ali, he was not content with simply demanding tribute, but destroyed all the old systems, and reconstructed them, giving their administration into the hands of his own functionaries.
cards.apply_it: For something you lead, write down who is responsible for each part. Fill any gap you find.

quiz.question: How did Askia's approach to conquered lands differ from Sunni Ali's?
options: He left local rulers fully in charge
He abandoned them after taking tribute
He let the scholars govern them
He rebuilt their administration with his own officials
quiz.explanation: Rather than just collecting tribute, he replaced the old systems with officials answerable to him.

cards.title: A standing army let Songhai's farmers and traders get on with their work
cards.body:
Sunni Ali had pulled almost everyone into his wars. Askia Mohammed, the Tarikh says, divided his people into subjects and soldiers. He built a professional army: cavalry with spears on strong horses, archers and armoured chiefs, and later units drawn from conquered peoples.

Dubois points to the side effect. With fighting left to soldiers, farmers and merchants could work without being called away, and commerce grew remarkably.

Specialisation frees people to do what they are good at. In a team or a household, too, asking everyone to drop everything for every crisis wears down the work that keeps things going.
cards.quote: The division of the population into civil and military classes permitted the productive and trading elements to pursue their occupations undisturbed. Commerce developed amazingly,
cards.apply_it: Is everyone around you pulled into every emergency? Decide who handles crises so others can keep the core work going.

quiz.question: What benefit did Askia's standing army bring beyond warfare?
options: Farmers and traders could work without being taken for war
quiz.explanation: Separating soldiers from civilians let the productive and trading classes carry on undisturbed, and trade grew.

cards.title: Standard weights and market inspectors made Songhai's trade trustworthy
cards.body:
Under Askia Mohammed, weights and measures were made uniform across the empire. Cheating was punished severely, and every important market had an inspector.

The work was divided too: Djenné handled trade inside the empire, Timbuktu dealt with Morocco and the north-west, and Gao with Egypt and Tripoli to the north-east. Dubois says Timbuktu, more than any town, gained from Askia's security and market rules, and caravans came in growing numbers.

Trade runs on trust. When buyers know a measure is a measure and cheats get caught, deals get faster and more frequent. Clear standards and honest checks are good for everyone except fraudsters.
cards.quote: A unification of weights and measures was decreed, and all falsifications were severely punished, every market of importance being placed under the surveillance of an inspector.
cards.apply_it: Where in your work could a clear, shared standard (a checklist, a price list, a definition) save arguments and build trust?

quiz.question: Which measure did Askia take to protect honest trade?
options: Making weights and measures uniform and placing inspectors in markets
quiz.explanation: He unified weights and measures, punished falsification and put inspectors in every important market.

cards.title: Askia took sound advice from a zealot; weigh the adviser as well as the advice
cards.body:
Among Askia Mohammed's counsellors was al-Maghili (Dubois writes El Moucheïli), a scholar from Tlemcen in present-day Algeria. Askia put questions to him on trade, fraud, land tax, inheritance and public morals.

Some answers were sound, such as appointing market inspectors and checking weights and measures. But al-Maghili had earlier stirred up violence against the Jewish community of Tuat in the Sahara and fled after the killings. Dubois notes that much of his advice carried the same harshness, often prescribing death.

Clever people can give good advice and bad advice at once. Take the useful parts, and look hard at the character and record of whoever offers it.
cards.quote: El Moucheïli counsels, among other things, the creation of inspectors of markets and manners, and the verification of weights and measures.
cards.apply_it: Think of an adviser or source you rely on. Which of their ideas would you still accept if someone else had said it?

quiz.question: What does Dubois say about al-Maghili's advice to Askia?
options: Some of it was sound, but much reflected his severity and intolerance
It dealt only with prayer times
quiz.explanation: He proposed useful market reforms, but also very harsh measures in keeping with his earlier persecution in Tuat.

cards.title: Timbuktu became a great centre of Islamic learning
cards.body:
Timbuktu had no stone, wood or good clay for grand buildings, so it put its energy into learning instead. Under the Askias in the 1500s, scholars gathered around the Sankore mosque, founded by a wealthy woman. Students came from the desert, Morocco and all over West Africa, and Arabic served as a shared language among many peoples.

Dubois calls it a younger sister of the universities of Cairo, Córdoba, Fez and Damascus. A local proverb sums up how people saw it.

A city with few natural advantages can still lead in something. Here, what made Timbuktu famous was the people and books it gathered rather than its buildings.
cards.quote: Salt comes from the north, gold from the south, and silver from the country of the white men, but the word of God and the treasures of wisdom are only to be found in Timbuctoo,
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The University of Sankoré ¶3
cards.apply_it: What is one thing you could become known for that does not depend on resources you lack?

quiz.question: According to the Sudanese proverb, what could only be found in Timbuktu?
options: The word of God and the treasures of wisdom
quiz.explanation: Salt came from the north and gold from the south, but wisdom and the word of God were said to be found only in Timbuktu.

cards.title: A Timbuktu scholar's day ran on teaching, service and prayer
cards.body:
The chronicles preserve the daily routine of Mohammed ben Abou Bakr, one of Timbuktu's most respected scholars. He lectured from early morning until ten. After going home to pray he went to the judge to handle his clients' cases and settle disputes. He led the midday prayer, taught at home until three, prayed again, taught somewhere else until dusk, and gave a last lecture in the mosque after sunset.

The day was full, but it had a clear rhythm, with prayer times acting as fixed breaks between blocks of different work.

Anchoring your day to a few fixed points, such as meals, a walk or a set start time, can make a heavy load easier to carry.
cards.quote: He gave lectures on different subjects from early morning until ten o’clock. After returning home for prayer he went to the kadi to settle the affairs of his clients and act as mediator between disputants.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The University of Sankoré ¶29
cards.apply_it: Pick three fixed anchors for tomorrow and plan your work in the blocks between them.

quiz.question: What structured Mohammed ben Abou Bakr's working day?
options: Fixed prayer times between blocks of teaching and legal work
quiz.explanation: The prayer times divided his day into blocks of lectures, legal work and more teaching.

cards.title: Timbuktu's scholars loved books and lent them freely
cards.body:
Books were a major trade in Timbuktu. Leo Africanus, quoted by Dubois, said more profit was made from books than from any other goods. Scholars hunted for volumes they lacked and copied by hand those they could not afford, building libraries of seven hundred to two thousand works.

They also shared. One scholar, Abou Bakr, lent his most treasured books to any student who asked and never asked for them back, though he loved them dearly. Over time he gave away his whole library this way.

Knowledge grows when it moves. Lending a book, sharing notes or explaining what you know costs little and can change someone's path.
cards.quote: He would lend them his most cherished books and never ask for them back again, however rare they might be. He lavished his entire library in this manner (may Allah reward him!); the student who came to his door to borrow was never denied,
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The University of Sankoré ¶34
cards.apply_it: Lend or give away one book that shaped you to someone who would benefit from it.

quiz.question: What was remarkable about the scholar Abou Bakr?
options: He refused to let anyone touch his books
He burned books he disagreed with
He lent his treasured books freely and never asked for them back
He sold books at high prices
quiz.explanation: He gave away his entire library by lending to any student who came, despite loving his books.

cards.title: Judge al-Aqib spoke as frankly to the sultan as to anyone
cards.body:
Timbuktu's scholars often acted as the conscience of the town. The chronicles praise the judge al-Aqib (Dubois writes El Akib) for his firmness and independence. He gave the sultan his opinion as frankly as he would to the humblest person. When he saw something in the ruler's conduct that the law condemned, he resigned his post and went home rather than go along with it.

Dubois adds that this habit drew the scholars into politics, which later cost them dearly.

Saying the same thing to the powerful as to everyone else is hard and sometimes costly. It is also what makes your word worth having.
cards.quote: possessed a mixture of firmness and independence which raised him above all prejudices; he expressed his opinion to the sultan with the same frankness he employed to his humblest subject.
cards.apply_it: Is there something you would say to a peer that you are holding back from someone senior? Find a respectful way to say it.

quiz.question: What would Judge al-Aqib do when the sultan acted against the law?
quiz.explanation: He spoke openly and, when the ruler's conduct broke the law, he gave up his post rather than condone it.

cards.title: A widow hid a history book in a mound to save it from those it shamed
cards.body:
Mahmud Kati (Dubois writes Mohammed Koti), born around 1460, was a scholar and counsellor of Askia Mohammed. He wrote a history of Ghana, Songhai and Timbuktu up to 1554, known as the Tarikh al-Fattash. In Dubois's day only fragments could be found.

A descendant told Dubois why. The book had recorded the humble origins of families who later became powerful, so they bought up copies and destroyed them. One of Kati's great-aunts saved the original by burying it in a box under a mound, telling visitors it was her ancestor's grave. A friend betrayed the secret, soldiers dug it up, and the book was lost when a canoe overturned.

Honest records can make powerful enemies. Protecting them takes care and trust.
cards.quote: Families, since grown rich and powerful, and the chiefs of various countries, were shown with very humble origins, sometimes being the offspring of slaves. The book caused great annoyance to many people on this account, and those interested bought all the copies they could procure
cards.apply_it: Is there an important record (family stories, photos, documents) that exists in only one place? Make a copy today.

quiz.question: Why did some families destroy copies of Mahmud Kati's history, according to his descendant?
options: It contained errors about the kings
It was written in a foreign language
quiz.explanation: The book showed that some newly powerful families came from humble beginnings, so they tried to erase it.

cards.title: Askia the Great was overthrown by his own sons
cards.body:
After some thirty-five years on the throne, Askia Mohammed grew old and weak. His many sons were impatient to replace him. In 1529, by Dubois's dating, the eldest, Askia Musa, rebelled and deposed him at Gao. A series of violent family struggles followed.

A later ruler, his nephew, exiled the old king to a small island near Gao, where the chronicle says the frogs leapt around him. Only when another son, Askia Ismail, took power was he brought back to the palace, where he died in 1538.

Even the greatest builders need a plan for handing on what they built. Without clear succession, the people closest to power often fight over it.
cards.quote: Bankouri relegated him to the little island of Kankaka, to the west of that town, ‘where the frogs leaped around him,
cards.apply_it: If you lead something, who would take over tomorrow if you had to step away? Start that conversation.

quiz.question: What happened to Askia Mohammed in old age?
options: He was deposed by his son and later exiled to an island
quiz.explanation: His son Musa deposed him, a later ruler exiled him to an island, and another son eventually brought him home.

cards.title: Askia's system kept Songhai running despite careless heirs
cards.body:
Askia Mohammed's successors spent much of their energy on feuds, killings among relatives and pleasure. Dubois says they kept up campaigns to hold what they had but added no new reforms.

Yet the empire held. The administration, army and market rules that Askia had set up kept running for decades, and prosperity did not fall.

Good systems can outlast the people who run them badly. If you build clear roles, fair rules and working routines, what you made has a chance to survive a weak patch in leadership. It will not survive forever without care, but it buys time.
cards.quote: In spite of receiving no care from its rulers, the powerful machinery created and set in motion by Askia the Great still endured, so well had it been planned and so solidly was it built.
cards.apply_it: Document one process you run so well that someone else could keep it going without you.

quiz.question: Why did Songhai stay prosperous under Askia Mohammed's careless successors?
options: The system he built kept working
quiz.explanation: The machinery of government Askia created was so well planned that it endured without much care from his heirs.

cards.title: Timbuktu's traders ran on letters of credit and long-term trust
cards.body:
Dubois describes how Arab merchants in Timbuktu, from Morocco, Tuat and Tripoli, set up a form of banking. A traveller could get from them letters of credit valid across North Africa. They also gave goods on credit to the dioulas, travelling West African traders.

This took courage. There was no police force, and two or three years might pass before a debtor came back. Some never did, Dubois says, more often because of wars and dangerous roads than dishonesty.

Credit is trust stretched across time and distance. It makes big trade possible, and it carries real risk, so spread it carefully and expect some losses that are nobody's fault.
cards.quote: They introduced a system of banking, and the traveller could procure from them letters of credit for the whole of northern Africa.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. The Commerce and Life of Timbuctoo ¶29
cards.apply_it: Before you lend money or goods, decide in advance how much you could afford to lose if things go wrong.

quiz.question: Why did some debtors of Timbuktu's merchants never return, according to Dubois?
options: Wars and unsafe routes often prevented them
The merchants refused to accept payment
quiz.explanation: Dubois says non-repayment was due less to dishonesty than to frequent wars and insecure routes.

cards.title: Morocco's rulers coveted Songhai's salt mines and gold
cards.body:
Salt was the most precious trade good of the Sudan, and it came from Taghaza, deep in the Sahara. Taghaza belonged to Songhai, though it lay closer to Morocco.

In 1545 the sultan of Morocco claimed the mines. Askia Ishak I refused and sent Tuareg raiders to a Moroccan border town to show he would defend them, which bought about twenty years of quiet. A later sultan demanded rent. Askia Daoud sent a friendly letter and a gift of ten thousand mitkals of gold, and the sultan let the matter drop.

Each approach worked for a time, one by firmness and one by generosity, but a rich neighbour's appetite tends to come back.
cards.quote: In 1545 Mouley Mohammed El Kebir, the sultan of Morocco, sent an embassy to the king of the Songhois, claiming the mines of Thegazza, under the pretext that they were situated on his frontiers.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Moors in the Sudan ¶4
cards.apply_it: Is there a recurring demand you keep settling with a quick fix? Think about what a lasting answer would look like.

quiz.question: How did Askia Daoud answer Morocco's demand for rent on the salt mines?
options: He sent a friendly reply with a large gift of gold
He went to war at once
quiz.explanation: He refused tribute but sent a conciliatory message and ten thousand mitkals of gold, which satisfied the sultan.

cards.title: Al-Mansur's councillors warned him about the desert, then folded
cards.body:
In 1590 Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco told his council he meant to conquer the Sudan for its riches. The councillors objected: the desert was so waterless and vast that even birds lost their way.

Al-Mansur replied that poor merchants crossed it all the time, and that his guns would make victory easy against soldiers with spears. The council gave in, praising his wisdom with the line that the minds of princes are the princes of minds.

His gamble did win battles, but the colony that followed brought decades of ruin. A leader's confidence can quickly silence a room. If you lead, make it safe for people to keep disagreeing; if you advise, stand by a good objection.
cards.quote: So true is it that the minds of princes are the princes of minds.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Moors in the Sudan ¶10
cards.apply_it: At your next meeting, ask directly: what is the strongest reason not to do this?

quiz.question: How did al-Mansur's council respond after he answered their objections?
options: They gave in and flattered his judgment
quiz.explanation: Persuaded, they told him God had inspired him and that the minds of princes are the princes of minds.

cards.title: At Tondibi in 1591, guns broke the Songhai army
cards.body:
Al-Mansur's force was small but chosen with care: by Dubois's figures, about three thousand musketeers and a thousand other troops, under Judar Pasha. They crossed the Sahara and in early 1591 met Askia Ishak II at Tondibi on the Niger, in present-day Mali. The chronicle gives Songhai thirty thousand foot and twelve thousand horse.

Numbers did not help. The smoke and noise of firearms caused panic, and Songhai's lines collapsed almost at once. Many were killed, even those who cried out that they were fellow Muslims. Ishak fled and Gao fell without a fight.

A new technology can make old strength irrelevant overnight. Those who dismiss it as noise may find out too late.
cards.quote: The sudden shock of smoke, noise, and the hail of balls so terrified them, that many, thinking nothing could preserve them from such miracles, did not even attempt to fly.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Moors in the Sudan ¶13
cards.apply_it: What new tool or method in your field are you dismissing? Spend an hour learning how it works.

quiz.question: What decided the battle of Tondibi, according to Dubois?
options: A surprise attack by the Tuareg
quiz.explanation: The smoke, noise and gunfire panicked the much larger Songhai army, which collapsed almost at once.

cards.title: 'Security became fear': the chronicler's lament for Songhai
cards.body:
The Tarikh es-Sudan sums up what the Moroccan conquest meant. Under the Askias, it says, the Sudan matched the most favoured lands on earth for plenty, prosperity, safety and health. After 1591 all that turned around.

The Moroccan commander then hunted down the remaining Songhai royal family, and dozens were killed. Provinces broke away, raiders spread, and trade along the Niger suffered for generations.

Peace and order are easy to take for granted. Their value shows most clearly when they are lost, and rebuilding them takes far longer than breaking them.
cards.quote: But from this time everything was altered; security became fear, prosperity was changed into ruin, health into sickness and anguish, and men began to fight and pillage among themselves.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Moors in the Sudan ¶19
cards.apply_it: Name one stable thing in your life (health, a friendship, a routine) you take for granted. Do one thing to look after it today.

quiz.question: How does the Tarikh describe the change after the Moroccan conquest?
options: Security turned to fear and prosperity to ruin
quiz.explanation: The chronicle says security became fear, prosperity became ruin, and people turned to fighting and pillage.

cards.title: Exiled scholars told the sultan that both of them would face judgment
cards.body:
When Timbuktu rose against its Moroccan garrison, the pasha Mahmud blamed the scholars. In 1594, Dubois writes, he arrested many of them with their families and seized their wealth. Some were killed; the rest were marched in chains across the Sahara and imprisoned in Marrakesh.

They did not grovel. One, dying in exile, left a sealed letter for the sultan: you are the oppressor and I the oppressed, but we will both stand before the same Judge.

Power can take freedom, books and property. It cannot force anyone to agree that what was done was right. Calm, dignified truth-telling under pressure is a kind of strength.
cards.quote: Thou art the oppressor and I am the oppressed, but oppressor and oppressed alike shall stand before the Eternal Judge.
cards.apply_it: When someone with power over you treats you unfairly, write down calmly what is true, even if you never send it.

quiz.question: What message did a dying exiled scholar leave for the sultan?
options: A request to be buried in Morocco
That oppressor and oppressed would both face the Eternal Judge
quiz.explanation: His sealed letter named the sultan as oppressor and reminded him both would stand before God.

cards.title: Ahmed Baba taught in his captors' city and stayed humble about his rulings
cards.body:
Ahmed Baba, born in 1556 at Arawan north of Timbuktu, was already called 'the unique pearl of his time' when he was carried off to Morocco in chains. His fame grew there. Moroccan scholars pressed for his release in 1596, and he was led in triumph to the main mosque of Marrakesh.

He was asked to teach, and after first refusing he lectured on rhetoric, law and theology to large crowds. Judges brought him their hardest questions, and his answers were taken as final. Yet he said he looked at each question from every side and, trusting his own judgment little, asked God for help.

Real expertise often comes with this kind of humility: careful checking, and awareness of what you might miss.
cards.quote: I carefully examined from every point of view the questions asked me, and having little confidence in my own judgment I entreated the assistance of God, and the Lord graciously enlightened me.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important decision, list the strongest argument against your first instinct.

quiz.question: How did Ahmed Baba describe his approach to legal questions?
options: He examined them from every angle, distrusting his own judgment and asking God's help
quiz.explanation: He examined each question from every point of view and, with little confidence in his own judgment, sought God's help.

cards.title: Ahmed Baba made the sultan come out from behind his curtain
cards.body:
After his release, Ahmed Baba was received by Sultan al-Mansur, who spoke to him from behind a curtain, as was his custom. The scholar refused to talk to a hidden ruler and asked him to come out. Al-Mansur did.

Ahmed Baba then asked him plainly why he had sacked his house, taken his books and chained him, adding that the chains had made him fall from his camel and break his leg. He said 1,600 of his books had been seized, though he owned the fewest of all his friends. When the sultan offered a religious justification, Ahmed Baba answered it from the same tradition, and al-Mansur ended the audience.

Respectful, direct and well-argued speech can hold even the powerful to account.
cards.quote: What need had you to sack my house, steal my books, and put me into chains to bring me to Morocco? By means of those chains I fell from my camel and broke my leg.
cards.apply_it: Is there a wrong you have never named to the person who did it? Plan a calm, direct way to say it.

quiz.question: What did Ahmed Baba ask al-Mansur to do at the start of their meeting?
options: Come out from behind the curtain
quiz.explanation: He cited the Qur'an to say he would not speak to a ruler hidden behind a veil, and the sultan came out.

cards.title: Ahmed Baba never stopped longing for Timbuktu
cards.body:
Though he was famous and honoured in Marrakesh, Ahmed Baba was not allowed to leave while al-Mansur lived; Dubois says he was held about twelve years in all. He wept when he spoke of home and wrote verses asking travellers to carry his greetings to Timbuktu.

After the sultan's death he was finally allowed to return. At the farewell, when a Moroccan scholar blessed him with a verse promising he would be brought back, he pulled his hand away and prayed never to return. He died in Timbuktu in 1627, leaving many books, including a great biographical dictionary of scholars that helped later historians rebuild Timbuktu's past.

Success abroad does not erase the pull of home. Keeping that bond alive can carry a person through long exile.
cards.quote: O thou who goest to Gao, turn aside from thy path to breathe my name in Timbuctoo. Bear thither the greeting of an exile who sighs for the soil on which his friends and family reside.
cards.apply_it: Send a message to someone back home you have not spoken to in a while.

quiz.question: What did Ahmed Baba ask of travellers heading to Gao in his poem?
options: To carry his greetings to Timbuktu
quiz.explanation: He asked them to turn aside and say his name in Timbuktu, greeting the friends and family he missed.

cards.title: A colony ruled only for its gold fell into chaos
cards.body:
For about twenty years the Moroccan colony on the Niger worked reasonably well. Then, after al-Mansur's death in 1603, his successors cared only whether the gold convoys arrived. Reinforcements stopped by 1620.

From 1613 the soldiers chose their own pasha. Rival commanders deposed and killed each other: Dubois counts twenty governors between 1620 and 1650, some lasting months, weeks or a single day. Garrisons split into factions, and the descendants of the soldiers, who married into local families, became the Arma (Dubois calls them Roumas), ruling small patches along the river.

An organisation run from afar purely for what it can extract tends to rot. People notice when no one cares about anything but the takings.
cards.quote: In a period of thirty years, 1620 to 1650, twenty governors may be counted.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Moors in the Sudan ¶31
cards.apply_it: If you manage anything from a distance, schedule time to understand how it is really going, not just its numbers.

quiz.question: How many governors did the Moroccan colony have between 1620 and 1650, by Dubois's count?
quiz.explanation: Dubois counts twenty governors in thirty years, some ruling only a few days amid constant rivalries.

cards.title: Al-Sadi wrote the Tarikh es-Sudan so the past would not be forgotten
cards.body:
Abd al-Rahman al-Sadi was born in Timbuktu into a family of scholars. He became imam in Djenné and served the pashas as secretary and envoy. In the 1650s he wrote the Tarikh es-Sudan, the history of Songhai, Timbuktu and Djenné that Dubois relied on.

In his preface he says that his ancestors loved recording the deeds of kings and scholars, but nobody in his own time cared. Seeing this precious knowledge fading, he set down everything he had read, seen or heard. Dubois praises his clear style and his habit of giving both versions of a disputed event.

When no one else is keeping a record, writing down what you know can be a gift to people not yet born.
cards.quote: Witnessing the decline of this science (history), so precious on account of the instruction it offers to mankind, I have implored the assistance of God in writing down all that I have read, seen, or heard concerning the kings of the Sudan and the Songhoi people,
cards.apply_it: Ask an older relative about one event from their life and write it down.

quiz.question: Why did al-Sadi say he wrote the Tarikh es-Sudan?
options: To prove Songhai came from Egypt
He saw interest in history declining and wanted to preserve it
quiz.explanation: He noticed no one in his time cared about history any more, so he recorded everything he knew.

cards.title: Ahmed Baba taught the value of facts and dates, and dates expose forgeries
cards.body:
Timbuktu's later scholars told Dubois that Ahmed Baba had taught them the importance of facts and dates. Dubois gives an example from Ahmed Baba's biographical dictionary.

A man once brought a ruler a document said to come from the Prophet, exempting a town from tax, signed by famous witnesses. Everyone was impressed until a sharp-memoried scholar looked at the names. One witness had not yet become a Muslim at the time, and another had already died. The document was a fake.

Checking whether the dates and people in a story line up is one of the simplest tests for truth. It still works on doctored quotes and fake news today.
cards.quote: He reflected a moment, then said, ‘All this is a lie.
cards.apply_it: Next time a quote or claim goes viral, check when it was supposedly said and whether the people named could have been there.

quiz.question: How did the scholar show the tax-exemption document was forged?
options: It was in the wrong language
The witnesses' dates did not fit: one was not yet Muslim and one had died
quiz.explanation: He noticed one witness converted only after the event and another had died before it, so the document could not be genuine.
